Extraction: Intelligent Site Reliability Engineering: A Multi-agent LLM Framework for Automated Incident Analysis and Root Cause Determination (title page, p. 1).
Vipin Kataria (Picarro Inc, USA; corresponding e-mail vipink2@illinois.edu) — single-author industry paper (p. 1).

2025 — International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems (IJIES), Vol. 18, No. 11, pp. 450-466, DOI 10.22266/ijies2025.1231.28; received 2025-09-04, revised 2025-10-14; CC BY-SA 4.0 license (header, p. 1). Modern distributed systems generate 10,000-50,000 daily alerts, causing alert fatigue and delayed incident response; SRE teams spend 60-80% of their time on manual investigation, and MTTR inflates from a typical 30-45 minutes to over 2-3 hours for complex distributed failures (§1, p. 1). Threshold-based alerting yields 60-85% false positives in dynamic cloud environments, manual correlation does not scale beyond 100-200 microservices, and traditional ML-based AIOps reaches only 45-65% root-cause accuracy because it pattern-matches without semantic understanding (§1, p. 2; §2.2, p. 3). Existing single-LLM operational tools lack the specialized domain expertise needed across logs, metrics, traces and infrastructure (§2.5, p. 4).

The Intelligent SRE Agent: a hierarchical four-layer multi-agent LLM framework in which an LLM-powered Master Agent (Claude-4 Sonnet) performs natural-language reasoning and investigation planning and orchestrates five domain-specialized agents — Logs, Metrics, Traces, Infrastructure and ML Services — via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) (§3.1, p. 4). Orchestration is prompt-driven and adaptive (planning, agent selection, introspection), with empirically observed confidence thresholds above 0.85 and 3-7 investigation rounds (§3.3, pp. 5-6); a four-phase workflow goes from alert interpretation to a diagnostic report with root cause, confidence scores and remediation recommendations (§3.7, p. 7). The agentic role is explicitly a copilot: default deployment is read-only advisory mode, with human-in-the-loop approval for P0/P1 incidents, hallucination mitigation via confidence scoring (<0.7 flagged), minimum 3-agent cross-validation, evidence grounding, circuit breakers and audit logging (§3.8, pp. 7-8).

Empirical dual-testbed evaluation with systematic chaos engineering: a primary controlled testbed (7-microservice IoT sensor pipeline, 150 injected failure scenarios over 8 weeks, 1,000 concurrent connections, single AWS region) and an extended production-replica staging environment (50+ microservices, 200 scenarios over 10 weeks, 5,000 connections, multi-AZ, heterogeneous stack) (§4.1, Table 1, p. 8). Failures were injected with Toxiproxy, Chaos Monkey, Litmus Chaos and custom injection (Table 2, p. 9) across five categories: infrastructure, application services, data pipeline, external dependencies and configuration (Table 3, p. 9). Executed baseline: parallel manual incident analysis by three senior SRE engineers (5+ years of distributed-systems experience), each incident analyzed independently by all three with consensus-based ground truth (§4.1.3 'Baseline Comparison', p. 10). Cross-LLM validation replicated the framework over Claude-4 Sonnet, GPT-4 Turbo, Gemini Pro and Llama-3-70B (Table 9, p. 13).

MTTD is measured directly as Mean Time to Diagnosis against an executed manual baseline (Art. I satisfied): 47.2 min (manual, 3 senior SREs) reduced to 8.5 min in the primary testbed — the 82% reduction claimed in the abstract and conclusion (Abstract, p. 1; §5.1, p. 14) — and to 11.2 min in the extended 50+ microservice validation, reported as a 79.1% overall reduction across both testbeds (Table 4, p. 10). Root-cause accuracy rose from 67.3% (manual) to 92.1% (primary) and 89.4% (extended); historical incident-matching precision from 43.1% to 96.3%/93.7%; false-positive rate fell from 28.7% to 4.2%/6.8% (Table 4, p. 10). Case studies show 8.3-16.4 min automated diagnosis vs 45-142 min manual (79.1-88.5% improvement; Table 7, p. 12), and per-category MTTD of 6.2-15.9 min (Table 5, p. 10). MTTR proper (time to resolution) is NOT measured — it appears only as motivating context (30-45 min to 2-3 h, §1, p. 1); the benefit evidenced is on the diagnosis stage of the incident-response pipeline.

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: Claims the first multi-agent LLM framework designed specifically for comprehensive incident analysis in distributed systems, with MCP-based dynamic orchestration as a reusable architectural pattern (§1 contributions, p. 2). Provides comparative evidence that domain specialization outperforms single-LLM AIOps (92.1% vs ~60-80% for single-model frameworks; Table 8, pp. 12-13) and that the architecture abstracts the underlying model: accuracy 84.2-92.1% and agent-coordination success 92.3-98.7% across four LLM providers (Table 9, p. 13), supporting vendor-independent deployment. Its production-safety stack (confidence scoring, multi-agent validation, evidence grounding, human-in-the-loop, advisory-first staged rollout; §3.8, pp. 7-8) is a concrete blueprint for operating agentic AI in critical infrastructure.

Scaling from 7 to 50+ microservices degrades performance (-2.7 pp accuracy, +2.7 min diagnosis time; §5.2, p. 14); external-dependency failures have the lowest accuracy (85.3-88.0%; Table 5, p. 10); the Traces Agent suffers the largest scalability impact (+74% response time; Table 6, p. 11; §5.2, p. 14); and the LLM-driven orchestration lacks a formal theoretical model, with non-deterministic behavior validated only empirically (§3.3, pp. 5-6; §5.2, p. 14). Additional caveats: evaluation uses injected failures on controlled/staging testbeds, not live production incidents (Table 1, p. 8); single-author industry paper; MTTR end-to-end is not measured. Future work: formal mathematical models of coordination, validation at 100+ microservices, advanced adversarial/hallucination safeguards, predictive incident prevention, and federated learning across organizations (§5.4, p. 14).

Direct and central: it is one of the four primary studies in the review's nominal MTTD/MTTR cluster backed by an executed baseline comparison, quantifying an agentic multi-agent LLM copilot that cuts MTTD by 82% (47.2 -> 8.5 min) against a concrete manual baseline of three senior SREs (Table 4, p. 10; Abstract, p. 1). Its human-in-the-loop, advisory-first deployment model (§3.8.3-3.8.4, p. 8) matches the thesis framing of a copilot (not autopilot) for incident response, and its MCP orchestration and safety mechanisms inform the thesis architecture discussion. Mandatory stratum caveat (PDR-0007): IJIES is NOT INDEXED in the review's quality strata, so its evidence is weighted accordingly; note also that the gain is on MTTD (diagnosis), with MTTR not directly measured.

High — it is one of the few included primaries with an executed empirical baseline (3 senior SREs, consensus ground truth) and explicit MTTD quantification (-82%, Table 4, p. 10) for an agentic LLM copilot in incident response, the exact phenomenon of the thesis. Weight is tempered by the non-indexed venue (PDR-0007) and testbed-only (non-production) validation.
